question: How does Adam differ from plain gradient descent and from momentum-based methods?
direct_answer: Adam combines momentum-like first-moment smoothing with adaptive per-parameter step sizes based on second-moment estimates.
expanded_answer: Plain gradient descent uses the current gradient directly with one global learning rate. Momentum adds an exponentially smoothed history of gradients to reduce noise and accelerate consistent progress. Adam goes further by tracking both a smoothed gradient and a smoothed estimate of gradient magnitude, then normalizing updates per parameter. This makes Adam adapt the step size differently for each parameter, which is especially useful when gradients have very different scales.
key_points: GD: direct gradient with one learning rate
Adam: momentum plus adaptive per-parameter scaling
Useful when gradients differ in scale across parameters
common_wrong_ideas: Adam is just momentum with a different name
Adam removes the need to tune any hyperparameters
Adaptive methods always outperform SGD in every setting
